title: do-release-upgrade insufficient disk space workaround
body:
do-release-upgrade checks if there’s enough disk space to complete the release upgrade, in my case to 26.04. If it finds that there isn’t enough, it quits and asks you to free some space, then try again. In my case, there’s not too much I can delete. Also, I have only one partition, so linking space on the home partition to /var/cache/apt won’t work. AI suggested that I mount a USB and link to that, and although it seems that it should work, it just doesn’t. I suspect what is going on is that do-release-upgrade blindly checks the root partition, which hasn’t grown one bit because of this trick. It doesn’t realize that all these temporary.deb files will go to the USB, and therefore not fill up the root partition. And AI doesn’t realize this, and incorrectly assumes that a simple link will solve the problem. The second thing that AI suggested was to pass a -o option to do-release-upgrade, overriding the name of the apt cache directory. At first glance, one would think that this will work. In fact, it does work for apt-get. The .deb files land on the USB drive, and the light even flashes to give the user a sense of security. But it doesn’t work with do-release-upgrade. The light never illuminates, and the upgrade fails yet again. AI is quick to explain that do-release-upgrade is known to be buggy, and routinely ignores options and environment variables. AI also suggested that I try setting an environment variable for the alternate cache location, making sure to use sudo -E to pass it to do-release-upgrade. This turned out not to work either. Although it could have been due to the possibility that do-release-upgrade simplistically only checks the root partition free space, ignoring the lessened requirements due to relocating the cache. Once, I thought I would be lost in such a complex situation without AI, but alas, it’s final suggestion to recover space by compressing logs, removing temporary upgrade files and old snaps ended up working, but just barely.

There’s got to be a better way!!!! Here’s an idea. Find a large directory with ncpd or something like that. Copy the files to USB, remove them from the root partition, and relink to the USB. This will truly reduce the space used in the root partition. The problem is that the files will be gone for a short while, and the system could go down. Is there anything that can safely be moved for a few seconds while the link executes? How about snap storage. I found this can take up a lot of space. I don’t think that the solution resides in deconstructing or fixing do-release-upgrade. Just try to work around its limitations. Might this work?

title: Move snap's multi-GB subdir "/var/lib/snapd/snaps" to different partition, then symlink to it?
body:
I have "only" a 64 Gigabyte root partition, /, hence implicitly the /var dir is on this partition, and so is snap's multi-GB subdir /var/lib/snapd/snaps . Snap stores the snap images in this directory. This takes quite some disk space.

I have freshly installed these snaps: boxy-svg, core, core18, core20, core22, eclipse, fx, gnome-3-34-1804, gnome-3-38-2004, go, gtk-common-themes, inkscape, minizinc, postman, powershell, rustup, slack, snapd, tidy, youtube-dl, zoom-client, and they already need 2,7G for a single-instance install. For backups this will increase to 10 GB quickly, because snap stores images of the 2 previous images too, in the long run.

I want to move these 10 GB on /var/lib/snapd/snaps to a different partition, on a different SSD. How can I do that properly?

I've tried by

  1. just by stopping snapd with sysctl,
  2. move /var/lib/snapd/snaps to a different partition
  3. symlinking to that partition ln -s /mnt/big-disk/snaps /var/lib/snapd/snaps
    1, restart snapd

However, this construct does not "survive" reboots (snaps cannot be mounted during startup), and also the snaps cannot be updated easily. As a workaround I've tried scripting commands such as
mount /var/lib/snapd/snaps/inkscape_10426.snap /snap/inkscape/10426
(with /var/lib/snapd/snaps/ being a symlink), but these are a nightmare to maintain, because the release ids such as 10426 always change.

title: Ubuntu default Firefox app won't start after system changes
body:
First question, I'm new to this site so apologies if it's an old chestnut.

I recently got pop-up warnings from the OS (Ubuntu 22.04) telling me that the root filesystem (/, mounted on /dev/sda1) was running low on disc space. I copied /home (the major culprit) to another internal disk which had plenty of free space and deleted /home from the boot disk. I then made a soft link from a new /home on /dev/sda1 to the copy of /home on the other disk. Things mostly work OK but when I try to start Firefox I get:

robin~$cannot perform operation: mount --rbind /home /tmp/snap.rootfs_G5r0Tf//home: Permission denied

I've done some research and it looks like this is something to do Firefox being a snap package. I've read a number of complaints about 'Permission denied' errors with snap. I'm probably going to upgrade my computer and start again with a fresh Linux (of some flavour) install, but I'd be grateful if anyone could shed light on what's going here and if possible suggest a workaround with my current setup. Robin
